extracted.intended_audience: mathematics and computer-science students and authors (students in a mathematical/technical writing course)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for writing mathematics, proofs, exercises, algorithms, and literate-programming documentation, with advice on typesetting, notation, module structure, and editing/revision practices. Aimed at producing clear, consistent, and reader-focused technical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place words between adjacent formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember to place words between adjacent formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions like the particularly bad example “Add p k times to c.” — put some words between adjacent formula fragments so the sentence reads naturally and unambiguously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define symbols before use
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to define symbols before you use them (or at least to define them very near where you use them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a symbol appears without definition the reader is confused. Either introduce the symbol earlier or define it immediately when first used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monotonous sentence openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t get hung up on one or two styles of sentences; repetitive openings become monotonous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of monotony: Thus, —; Consequently, —; Therefore, —; And so, —. Vary sentence structure and openings; but use parallelism when that is the rhetorical point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sentences comprehensible left-to-right
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to make sentences easily comprehensible from left to right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: “We prove that hgrunti and hsnorti implies hblahi.” Better: “We prove that the two conditions hgrunti and hsnorti imply hblahi.” Otherwise readers may misparse which items are being proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place 'that' by cadence and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The final placement of the word 'that' must be dictated by cadence and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read sentences aloud to decide whether to include/move 'that' for best rhythm and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'shall' in definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'shall' seems natural for definitions to many mathematical readers, but it is considered formal by younger members of the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of audience expectations; choose tone accordingly when writing definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise in wording (logical negation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be precise in your wording. If you mean “not nonincreasing,” don’t say “increasing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two mean different things: 'not nonincreasing' means there exists j with p_j < p_{j+1}, while 'increasing' means p_j < p_{j+1} for all j. Choose words to match precise mathematical meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixed tenses on the same subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed tenses on the same subject are awkward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer consistent tense: e.g., “We assume now hgrunti, hoping to show a contradiction,” rather than mixing future and present constructions awkwardly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clear phrasing for proofs by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the ungainly phrase “Assume by contradiction that ...”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better: “The proof that hblahi is by contradiction.” Even better: “To prove hgrunti, let us assume the opposite and see what happens.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conversational tone with signposts
rubrics_metrics.description: A conversational tone giving signposts and clearly written transition paragraphs provides for pleasant reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short asides or explicit guidance to the reader (e.g., “The operative word is zero,” “The lemma is half proved,” “We divide the proof into two parts...”) to improve readability and motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep relational expressions consistent and readable
rubrics_metrics.description: You can give relations in two ways, either saying ‘p_i < p_j’ or ‘p_j > p_i’; keep indices in consistent relative positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the form easiest for the reader to visualize given your earlier notation (e.g., after you said p = (p1, p2, ..., pn) and i < j). Avoid mixing order like ‘i < j and p_j < p_i’ which breaks positional consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise in multiple passes; prefer handwritten first pass
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical rewrite sequence: first copy in pencil; type it, editing for flow during typing; then TEX and further passes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don writes in pencil because handwriting pace matches thinking; typing interrupts flow. Rewriting occurs across stages — different passes reveal different issues. Expect many drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use professionals for book production
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not forget the value of professionals: book designers and copy editors are worth their keep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers decide margins, fonts, chapter headings; copy editors catch punctuation and style slips. Consider leaving room for 'graffiti' (marginal snappy comments) if the designer allows it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put reasons before rules for reader expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a rule will provoke reader curiosity, tell them why first and then state the rule's significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example Before/After: move ‘it is particularly valuable because ...’ before naming the rule to avoid readers wondering 'why' while reading the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose phrasing to avoid awkward repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid constructions that repeat the same words awkwardly (e.g., ‘by replacing –– by ––’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If repetition occurs, change words (e.g., ‘by changing –– to ––’) to improve flow and avoid clumsy repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read at normal speed to check rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, try reading at speed to sense the rhythm of the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud or at normal reading speed helps spot rhythmic and flow problems not obvious when composing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not display false equations as standalone displays
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a bad idea to display false equations; the reader may take them as gospel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need to show a false equation, put it into the text quoted: “So the equation ‘...’ is always false!” rather than centering it as a display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure clear antecedents for pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure that the antecedent of any pronoun that you use is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sentences starting with 'It is ...' that leave 'it' ambiguous. Sometimes rephrase to 'Two things about this derivation are worthy of note. First, we see again...' to make antecedents clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid page breaks splitting displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Towards the end of editing ensure you don’t have a page break in the middle of a displayed formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If necessary, add or change surrounding text to move the display entirely to the next page; treat this as an editing opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let proofs follow the same order as definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Let proofs follow the same order as definitions, especially when dealing with several separate cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize proofs in the same sequence as related definitions so the reader can follow the structure naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hyphens, en-dashes, minus signs, and em-dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphens, dashes, and minus signs are distinct and should not be used interchangeably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hyphen (-) for compound words, en-dash (–) for ranges like 'lines 10–18', minus sign (−) in formulas, and em-dash (—) for sentence breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread for mathematics as well as prose
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofreading you may catch technical errors as well as stylistic errors. Think about the mathematics too, not just the prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: revise statements like 'when x → 0' to 'when x decreases to 0' if negative approaches make expressions undefined. Mathematical accuracy matters in copyediting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise with contrast words like 'instead'
rubrics_metrics.description: When you use the word ‘instead’, be clear about the contrast you are drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'And when x = −1 instead, ...' Better: 'And when x = −1 instead of +1, ...' — make the alternative explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use present tense for timeless facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the present tense for timeless facts; things proved earlier are still true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use past tense only for 'facts' that turned out to be in error or truly time-bound statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repeating words in a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to avoid repeating words in a sentence; choose alternate words where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: change 'fill in the values' to 'fill in the entries' to avoid repetition and increase clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give page numbers only for remote references
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually give page numbers only for remote references (to equations, say); for nearby references 'using Equation 5.14' is enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page numbers become unwieldy if used for every reference; prefer equation/table labels or local references. The 'freeway method'—numbering tables by page number—may be useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose notation forms by space and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose whether integral limits go above/below or at the right based on horizontal vs vertical space; be consistent throughout the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Putting limits above and below trades vertical space for horizontal; both forms are used — decide one form per work for consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break long formulas logically; author decides display
rubrics_metrics.description: When long formulas don’t fit, try to break the lines logically; the author can change the math (introduce a symbol) to make placement less jarring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should decide how to display complex expressions; changing math for presentation is acceptable when it improves exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedded vs displayed formula line-break convention
rubrics_metrics.description: The placement of the equals sign (=) is different for line breaks in embedded versus displayed formulas: break comes after the equals in an embedded formula, but before the equals in a display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this convention to keep breaks look logical and consistent with typographic norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use punctuation changes to affect flow
rubrics_metrics.description: While editing for flow, sentences can be broken up by changing semicolons to periods or periods to semicolons; break paragraphs into smaller ones as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust punctuation and paragraphing deliberately to control reading speed and emphasis, but preserve clarity (especially for sentences starting with conjunctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure variable names are not misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure your variable names are not misleading; names too similar to unrelated variables confuse readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic variable renaming (one advantage of editors) to keep names meaningful and distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer slash form for complicated fractions in running text
rubrics_metrics.description: Overuse of stacked fractions with horizontal bars can produce tiny characters (especially in exponents); prefer the slash form (1 + x)/y when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy editors often 'slash' fractions and add parentheses where needed; consider this when writing to avoid badly rendered tiny numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises require clarity and redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises are difficult to write because they have little context; ambiguity can be especially deadly, so carefully chosen redundancy is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make exercises self-contained; add clarifying phrases even if slightly redundant. This also aids accurate translation to other languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit sources for exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright law now makes it necessary to give credit to all previously published exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crediting sources is probably sufficient; tracing original attributions can be time-consuming but benefits future authors and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise answers may be pithy or start with symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: We can dispense with some rhetorical guidelines when writing answers to exercises: quick, pithy answers and answers that start with a symbol are acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise answers are allowed to be terse; context and pedagogical goals determine level of exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present algorithms in English and as labeled steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Don decided to write algorithms in English rather than in a specific programming language to avoid alienating readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present algorithms like Theorems with labeled steps and parenthetical comments (often invariants) — this aids understanding and formal reasoning about them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain complex things twice and modularly
rubrics_metrics.description: The correct way to explain a complex thing is to break it into parts and then explain each part; things should be explained twice (formally and informally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle supports literate programming: modules begin with informal text and finish with formal code (e.g., Pascal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce modules at the psychologically right moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Each module should be introduced at the psychologically right moment so the program can be written to motivate the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order modules to match the order a reader needs them; TANGLE/TEX can reorder for compilation, but exposition should be motivating and incremental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and be consistent in narrative voice for programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to use 'we' or 'it' when describing program behavior and be consistent; Don favors 'we'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency aids comprehension: if you adopt 'we insert the element...' keep that voice throughout rather than alternating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module naming: imperatives vs descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Students used descriptors and imperatives for module names; imperatives (e.g., 'Store the word in the dictionary') are often preferred unless the module is declarative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use descriptors for modules that are lists/declarations (e.g., 'Procedures for sorting'); capitalize the first letter of a module name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module should contain an informal clear description
rubrics_metrics.description: Each module should contain an informal but clear description of what it actually does; avoid play-by-play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a high-level intuition rather than a line-by-line recap; a play-by-play isn't as helpful for understanding the design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep modules short (about a dozen lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modules that are much too long should be cut into several pieces; about a dozen lines is a good module length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The WEB philosophy is to break complex things into tractable parts. Short modules are easier to read and reason about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'engineerese' and maintain good prose in module descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions that are all conjunctions and no punctuation ('engineerese') make poor documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write clear, punctuated, and descriptive module text; use descriptive variable names (e.g., caps_range instead of range) and avoid sloppy language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid carrying obsolete conventions into new styles
rubrics_metrics.description: When you change style (e.g., adopt WEB), don't carry excess baggage like unnecessary end{while} comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt conventions appropriate to the new system; remove redundant conventions that the new style renders unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use underscores in identifiers rather than CamelCase
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifiers like 'FindInNewWords' look bad in print; WEB allows a short underscore to conjoin words (e.g., get_word).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer underscores for readability in printed material; TANGLE will remove underscores for Pascal; avoid uppercase-lowercase mixes that were not designed for typography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use typewriter type for hexadecimal numbers and appropriate fonts for numeric literals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use typewriter type for hexadecimal numbers (e.g., '3F' in typewriter font) but leave decimal numeric literals in normal type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention looks appropriate and provides a subliminal type-checking cue to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with asterisks and multiplication symbols in typeset text
rubrics_metrics.description: Typeset asterisks tend to appear higher above the line than typewritten ones, so multiplication formulas may look strange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer × for multiplication or use a typewriter-style font with centered '*' characters rather than the typographic '*' in normal fonts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep related routines together in the exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: When a program uses a specialized data structure that might be unknown to readers, keep all routines for that structure together in the text so they can be read as a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WEB allows flexible ordering; group related material so it remains 'fresh in the reader's mind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Put begins/ends inside called modules, not in calling modules
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s a good idea to put your begins and ends inside the called modules, not putting them in the calling module; mixing conventions causes bugs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of preferred style: use a short module call if down = 4 then { Punt }; define the module with begin...end inside its own definition. Mixing styles can produce errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep error-handling code modular and referenced
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of burying long error-handling code in a routine, have a single line near the beginning that points to a separate module that handles errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This keeps the main module focused on normal cases and places error recovery where it feels natural to implement well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use italics for variable names in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: It is good practice to use italics for the names of variables when they appear in comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This visual distinction aids the reader in separating narrative from code identifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let variables in module title correspond to local parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the variables in the module title correspond to the local parameters in the module itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the module header communicates the parameters and matches the implementation to reduce reader confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between documentation and code terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: The words used in the documentation should match the words used in the formal program; using two different terms for the same thing confuses the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a single vocabulary across exposition and code to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'I' for anthropomorphized computer prompts is optional but must be intentional
rubrics_metrics.description: Don generally likes the use of ‘I’ by the computer when referring to itself (e.g., 'What file should I process?') as it helps users conceptualize actions; others (like Dijkstra) object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you anthropomorphize the computer, do so consistently and with awareness of audience preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be tolerant of personal style but maintain key conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal style that works for the author is valuable, but many people trying to imitate Don's style 'botch it' by ignoring conventions he deems most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop your own coherent style that includes the important conventions (clarity, module granularity, consistent notation) rather than superficially copying surface features.
